title: One act a week
hook: Sikhs call selfless service seva; Jews speak of chesed, Muslims of sadaqa, Christians of charity: different words, each with its own meaning

segments.voice: Yesterday, Compline and the words many traditions say at night. Your line was the day is done. Which line did you choose? Day one hundred thirty-eight.

In the kitchen of a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, the work is already under way. Someone is rolling out flatbread. Someone is washing a mountain of steel plates. Someone is looking after the shoes by the door. Some of them might be doctors or business owners; you can't tell, and nobody asks. They're serving a free meal to whoever walks in, of any faith or none. Ask what they're doing, and you may hear one word. A new week starts today, and it turns us outward, toward other people. Today's word is seva.
screen: `WASHING A MOUNTAIN OF PLATES.` → `WHOEVER WALKS IN IS FED.` → `SEVA.`

segments.voice: Seva means service, and for Sikhs it means selfless service: work done for others with no reward in mind. The Sikh Gurus taught that serving others is part of remembering God, not a break from it, and the free kitchen, the langar, is one of the places it happens. But this is a word with neighbors, and each neighbor has its own meaning. Jews speak of chesed, loving-kindness: acts of kindness, like visiting the sick or comforting mourners, done beyond what's strictly required. Muslims speak of sadaqa, voluntary charity; hadith collected in Sahih al-Bukhari call every good deed a charity, and a kind word a charity too. Christians speak of charity, which in the older English Bible translates the Greek word for love: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Four words. They aren't the same word in four languages, and it would flatten each of them to pretend so. What they share is a habit: turning your hands toward someone else, on purpose, over and over. And that's where this week lands. Not a single heroic day. A rhythm. One act of service a week, small enough to actually keep. A week gives you enough time to plan it and enough room to fit it in, and seven days from now you'll do it again.
screen: `SEVA: SELFLESS SERVICE.` · `CHESED, SADAQA, CHARITY.` · `EACH WITH ITS OWN MEANING.` · `A RHYTHM, NOT A HERO DAY.` · then, large: `ONE A WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan this week's one act. Settle, and breathe. Let a few faces come to mind: a neighbor, a relative, a coworker, a stranger's need you've walked past. Let one small act appear. An hour at a food bank. Groceries for someone who's unwell. Washing up somewhere that needs it. Pick one. Picture when you'll do it this week. See your hands doing it. The bell holds the time.
Seva. Selfless service, as Sikhs use the word, done for others with no reward in mind, often in the free kitchen. Today's word.
Your line: one a week. Today, write down this week's one act and the day you'll do it. That's all. Day one hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs do seva at the gurdwara, cooking and serving the free meal called langar, washing dishes or minding shoes, and volunteers of every faith and none keep weekly shifts at food banks and shelters.

myth: seva, chesed, sadaqa and charity all mean exactly the same thing
each has its own story and its own meaning; what they share is a habit.
the langar serves a free meal to anyone, of any faith or none
a hadith says even a kind word can be a charity
Sahih al-Bukhari records that a good word is a charity, and that every good deed is a charity.

fork.setup: you want service to become part of your life. what does this week suggest?
options: one big heroic day a year.
wait until you have more time.
fork.reveal: one small act a week: small enough to keep, regular enough to become a rhythm.

original.note: Gurmukhi, seva: service. the word comes from Sanskrit seva, and Sikhs use it for selfless service.

trapdoor: what you thought: seva is volunteering with a nicer name.
what it means: for Sikhs, selfless service is part of remembering God, often done in the langar.
what a scholar hears: 'charity' in the King James renders Greek agape, love; a hadith in Bukhari 6021 counts every good deed as charity.

notes: Sahih al-Bukhari 6021 ('every good deed is charity'); the 'kind word is charity' form is in Bukhari 2989: Islam Keeper to confirm numbers.
Chesed defined as loving-kindness beyond obligation, with visiting the sick and comforting mourners as examples: Jewish Keeper to confirm.
Sadaqa root s-d-q (truthfulness): confirm. Gurmukhi ਸੇਵਾ and Sanskrit origin: confirm.

Reviewer fix: the teach previously merged two hadith into one ('a hadith ... every good deed is a charity, even a kind word'); now attributed as two reports (6021, 2989). Also changed 'its own God behind it' to 'its own tradition behind it' so the script does not take a position on whether Jews, Christians and Muslims worship different Gods.
Seva is also a Hindu term; the script calls it 'the Sikh word' in the word segment. Sikh and Hindu Keepers may want 'as Sikhs use it'.
Seva is cited to Sikh practice generally; a Sikh Keeper may want to add the best-known Guru Granth Sahib passage on service, by Ang number.
